\section[\texorpdfstring{\mr{जिना} (jinā)}{जिना (jinā)}]{\mr{जिना} (jinā) — stairs}

\label{lesson:MR-C91-jina}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marathi for a cupboard, then the Marathi for the ground.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{जिना}}
\textbf{\mr{जिना}} — \emph{jinā} — \textquotedblleft{}stairs\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{जिना}} (\emph{jinā}) is a loan, usually traced to Persian \emph{zīna}, \textquotedblleft{}ladder, stairs\textquotedblright{}. Marathi writes the \emph{z} as \textbf{\mr{ज}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\mr{आरसा} (ārsā)}{आरसा (ārsā)}]{\mr{आरसा} (ārsā) — a mirror}

\label{lesson:MR-C91-arsa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marathi for the ground, then the Marathi for stairs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{आरसा}}
\textbf{\mr{आरसा}} — \emph{ārsā} — \textquotedblleft{}a mirror\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{आरसा}} (\emph{ārsā}) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from \emph{ādarśa}, \textquotedblleft{}mirror\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 1143). It is built on \emph{dṛś}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\mr{पंखा} (paṅkhā)}{पंखा (paṅkhā)}]{\mr{पंखा} (paṅkhā) — a fan}

\label{lesson:MR-C91-pankha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marathi for a mirror, then the Marathi for a lamp.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पंखा}}
\textbf{\mr{पंखा}} — \emph{paṅkhā} — \textquotedblleft{}a fan\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{पंखा}} (\emph{paṅkhā}) is a tadbhava of Sanskrit \emph{pakṣa}, \textquotedblleft{}wing, feather\textquotedblright{}, whose form \emph{pakṣaka} also meant \textquotedblleft{}fan\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7627). CDIAL lists Marathi \emph{pākh}, \textquotedblleft{}wing\textquotedblright{}, and suggests, with a query, that the nasal comes from a crossing with Sanskrit \emph{puṅkha}, \textquotedblleft{}the feathered end of an arrow\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\mr{किल्ली} (killī)}{किल्ली (killī)}]{\mr{किल्ली} (killī) — a key}

\label{lesson:MR-C91-killi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marathi for a lamp, then the Marathi for a fan.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{किल्ली}}
\textbf{\mr{किल्ली}} — \emph{killī} — \textquotedblleft{}a key\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{किल्ली}} (\emph{killī}) comes from \emph{*kīlla}, a form CDIAL reconstructs beside Sanskrit \emph{kīla}, \textquotedblleft{}stake, peg\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3202). CDIAL notes an Indo-European origin proposed for \emph{kīla}, but thinks its variant shapes support a non-Aryan one.
\end{cousinweb}
